hops.title: The Vermont rats that drink their body weight
hops.text: In 1961 a colony of Long-Evans rats in Brattleboro, Vermont, turned up animals that drank and urinated enormously. The trait was recessive, and those animals founded the Brattleboro strain. Homozygous rats drink 30 to 100 percent of their own body weight in water every day. In 1984 Schmale and Richter found the cause: a single deleted G in the vasopressin precursor gene, which shifts the reading frame. Without circulating vasopressin, collecting-duct cells lose the usual signal to put more aquaporin-2 into their membranes, so the rats pass huge volumes of dilute urine. With one of the loop's two effectors gone, drinking becomes their main defence of plasma osmolality.

sources.citation: Török B, Varga J, Zelena D. Vasopressin as a Possible Link between Sleep-Disturbances and Memory Problems. Int. J. Mol. Sci. 23(24):15467 (2022).

hops.title: How the eight-glasses-a-day rule may have started
hops.text: Most people have heard that healthy adults should drink eight 8-ounce glasses of water a day. In 2002 the Dartmouth physiologist Heinz Valtin looked for the studies behind the rule and found none. One suggested source is a 1945 U.S. Food and Nutrition Board recommendation of about 2.5 litres of water a day, which added that most of that amount is already in prepared food. If that is the origin, the second half of the advice got lost. For healthy, sedentary adults in a mild climate, coffee and tea count, and the threshold-and-gain system you just plotted, with thirst, keeps the books.

sources.citation: Valtin H. 'Drink at least eight glasses of water a day.' Really? Is there scientific evidence for '8 x 8'? Am. J. Physiol. Regul. Integr. Comp. Physiol. 283(5):R993–R1004 (2002).
Maroz N, Maroz U, Iqbal S, Aiyer R. Nonobstructive hydronephrosis due to social polydipsia: a case report. J. Med. Case Rep. 6:376 (2012).

image.caption: Valtin found no studies behind eight glasses a day for healthy, sedentary adults; food supplies much of our water.

hops.afterHeading: Thirst: acting before the blood changes
hops.title: How cold, fizzy water takes the edge off thirst
hops.text: Come in hot and thirsty, and cold seltzer takes the edge off fast. The blood is much slower: in a 1984 study of dehydrated adults who drank tap water, a change in serum osmolality was first detected 30 to 60 minutes later. In a 2016 study, adults who had gone without water overnight drank less extra water after 400 millilitres of cold or carbonated water than after room-temperature still water. Drinking through a straw from an opaque cup, people also estimated about 22 percent more for cold, fizzy water than for the same amount at room temperature. Cold in the mouth is one cue the brain seems to use.

sources.citation: Geelen G, Keil LC, Kravik SE, Wade CE, Thrasher TN, Barnes PR, Pyka G, Nesvig C, Greenleaf JE. Inhibition of plasma vasopressin after drinking in dehydrated humans. Am. J. Physiol. 247(6 Pt 2):R968–R971 (1984).

Peyrot des Gachons C, Avrillier J, Gleason M, Algarra L, Zhang S, Mura E, Nagai H, Breslin PAS. Oral Cooling and Carbonation Increase the Perception of Drinking and Thirst Quenching in Thirsty Adults. PLoS ONE 11(9):e0162261 (2016).

image.caption: After cold or fizzy water, thirsty adults drank less extra water when more was offered five minutes later.

audio.title: Sheep brains, steady bows and cold seltzer
audio.transcript: The hypothalamus steers the body through hormones in the blood and through nerves, and it can use clues about what is coming to start a response early. Here are three stories, one for each. First, the blood route. In the nineteen fifties and sixties, scientists were still arguing over whether the hypothalamus really controlled the anterior pituitary through hormones carried in tiny portal veins. Proving it meant catching one of those hormones. The trouble was that each brain holds only traces of the releasing hormones. To isolate enough thyrotropin-releasing hormone, or T R H, Roger Guillemin's team in Houston collected close to five hundred thousand sheep hypothalami from Texas slaughterhouses. Their separation columns stood so tall that technicians loading extracts at the top and collecting drops at the bottom had to talk by walkie-talkie. Meanwhile, his rival Andrew Schally worked through millions of pig hypothalamic fragments. From all that sheep tissue, Guillemin's lab ended up with one milligram of pure T R H, a tiny peptide of just three amino acids. Schally's lab, working independently with pig tissue, reached the same hormone, and in nineteen seventy-seven the two men shared half of the Nobel Prize. Now switch to the wired route: sympathetic nerves and the adrenal medulla. When a violinist steps onto a stage for a high-stakes orchestra audition, sympathetic outflow releases noradrenaline and the adrenal medulla pours adrenaline into the blood. Beta receptors carry two of the symptoms a violinist notices most: the racing heart and the fine tremor in the bow hand. In a survey published in nineteen eighty-eight, more than two thousand players from the International Conference of Symphony and Opera Musicians responded. Twenty-seven percent reported having used propranolol or another beta-blocker, and more than ninety-six percent of the occasional users said it eased their performance anxiety. Earlier, a nineteen eighty-two study of twenty-nine musicians across two trials included a blinded propranolol comparison. Blocking beta receptors reduced the physical effects of stage fright and earned better ratings from experienced music critics, without sedating the players. A shaky bow is not a character flaw. It is partly the sympathetic system doing its ordinary job. Finally, feedforward control, where the brain acts before your blood even shifts. In a nineteen eighty-four experiment on eight mildly dehydrated adults who drank tap water in about two minutes on average, plasma vasopressin dropped within three minutes and returned to hydrated levels by nine minutes. Yet the study detected no change in serum sodium or osmolality until thirty to sixty minutes after drinking. Three years later, a small study of four dehydrated volunteers compared sucking on ice chips for thirty minutes with sipping one hundred milliliters of water at twenty-five degrees Celsius. The ice chips lowered plasma vasopressin within ten minutes, even with no change in blood osmolality, while the room-temperature water did not. And in two thousand sixteen, thirsty adults who drank four hundred milliliters of cold or carbonated water went on to drink noticeably less extra water than after room-temperature still water. In a separate test with opaque cups and straws, people guessed they had swallowed about twenty-two percent more cold, fizzy water than room-temperature water, even though the servings were the same size. Signals from the mouth and throat can start turning down vasopressin before any change in the blood is measurable.
